John Rippon
JON RIP-uhn
proper noun
English surname, from a place-name in Yorkshire; the given name John from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”

📖 Biblical Definition

John Rippon (1751–1836) was a Particular Baptist pastor who, at twenty, succeeded John Gill at the Carter Lane meeting in London and shepherded that congregation for sixty-three years. He stood squarely in the doctrines of grace handed down through Gill and Keach, holding the sovereign electing love of God, particular redemption, and the free offer of the gospel together without apology. His enduring service to the church was not chiefly the pulpit but the hymnal: his Selection of Hymns from the Best Authors, first published in 1787, ran through edition after edition and shaped the praise of Baptist congregations for generations. In that Selection Rippon set before the saints “How Firm a Foundation,” a hymn built wholly upon the promises of God to His people, that He will never leave nor forsake them. Rippon also published a Baptist register that preserved the labors and obituaries of his brethren, valuing the memory of faithful men. He governed his flock as one persuaded that worship must be doctrinally sound, that the songs a people sing will teach them what they believe. His long ministry is a witness to perseverance: one man, one pulpit, one steady confession across six decades, feeding the same sheep until the Lord called him home.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An English Particular Baptist pastor and hymn-editor, successor to John Gill, who published “How Firm a Foundation” in his widely-used Selection of Hymns.

expand to see more

JOHN RIPPON, a Particular Baptist minister of London (1751–1836), pastor of the Carter Lane congregation for sixty-three years.

Succeeded John Gill at the age of twenty and held the same Calvinistic Baptist confession.

Editor of Rippon’s Selection of Hymns from the Best Authors (1787), a standard among Baptists for decades.

His Selection first gave the church the beloved hymn “How Firm a Foundation,” grounded in the unbreakable promises of God.

Published a Baptist register that recorded the lives and deaths of his fellow ministers.

📖 Key Scripture

Heb 13:5 — "Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee."

Isa 43:2 — "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee."

1Co 3:11 — "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ."

Psa 89:34 — "My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The danger is not a redefinition of Rippon but a forgetting of him: that a pastor’s greatest legacy may be the doctrinally sound songs he sets in the mouths of God’s people.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Rippon’s long labor is the unbreakable firmness of the divine foundation. “How Firm a Foundation” sings God’s own promises back to Him, and a generation that trades such promise-laden praise for shifting sentiment loses the very ground beneath its feet.

Rippon also rebukes our restlessness. Six decades in one pulpit is unfashionable in an age of constant reinvention, yet the slow, steady feeding of one flock is precisely the shepherd-work the Lord honors. Faithfulness, not novelty, is the measure of a true ministry.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The surname Rippon derives from the Yorkshire town of Ripon; the man’s name endures chiefly through the hymn-book he edited.

expand to see more

John Rippon — John, from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”

Rippon is a locative surname tied to the cathedral town of Ripon in Yorkshire.

His Selection became so common that “Rippon’s” was shorthand for the Baptist hymn-book.

“How Firm a Foundation” appeared anonymously in the 1787 edition, signed only with the letter “K.”

The Carter Lane congregation traced its line through Gill to the founders of the Particular Baptists.

Usage

"John Rippon gathered the best hymns of his age and gave them to the singing church."

"Few editors have served the saints as long or as well as John Rippon."

"When a congregation sings “How Firm a Foundation,” it sings from John Rippon’s Selection."
